paragraphs: President Donald Trump said in an interview broadcast Sunday on CBS's 60 Minutes that his deportation policy "might be too tough" and offered to strike an immigration deal with Democrats, according to The Guardian. The interview followed the Republicans' defeat in the midterm elections.

Asked by correspondent Ross Douthat whether the policy had gone too far, Trump said some people think it is great but "a lot of people think it's too tough." He said it "both helped and hurt," citing an "A+ for closing up the border" and high marks for removing "the bad ones." But he said he was hurt because agents also took people with good jobs whose only violation was entering the country illegally.

Trump said a deal was "doable." It would target killers, rapists and drug dealers while letting some people who have been here 10 or 15 years stay. He said some Democrats had already contacted him. The Democrats' response was not reported in the page text.

The Guardian noted that the remarks seemed at odds with Trump's decision on Friday to make Stephen Miller, the architect of the crackdown, White House chief of staff. It also reported that ICE raids have caught people with no criminal records, and that federal agents fatally shot two US citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis earlier this year.

On other subjects, Trump blamed the Iran war and higher gasoline prices for much of the midterm loss but said he would make the same decision on the war again. He called his economic message "bad messaging, maybe by me," and said of AI regulation: "I don't mind guardrails."

President Donald Trump said Sunday that he "was only kidding" when he announced a day earlier that he had offered the White House press secretary job to Dana White, the chief executive of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, according to The Guardian. Trump spoke to reporters on his way back to the White House from his beach club in Florida.

Trump explained the premise of the joke: if White, a devoted fan of the president, took over the briefing room flanked by six fighters, reporters "wouldn't mess around with him so much." He added: "So I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy." He said it was "just a little fun" and pointed to the fighters he had named as White's assistants as proof he was joking.

Trump also said the mock announcement was something where he was kidding, "and then people said, 'You know, that's actually a pretty good idea.'" According to The Guardian, he did not say who supported it.
The Guardian reported that earlier Sunday Trump shared an animated AI cartoon made by a supporter, showing UFC fighters beating up journalists.

The Guardian also noted that White has praised Trump publicly before. He appeared in the first of a series of taxpayer-funded White House ads that ran before the midterms, calling Trump "the toughest, most resilient human being I have ever met in my life." He used the same phrase during the 2024 campaign.

The press secretary job has been vacant for three weeks, the Guardian said, since Katie Zacharia resigned after questions about why she described herself as an attorney despite having failed the bar exam.

A 24-year-old man suspected of killing six people in a market square in Kraków, Poland, died in hospital early Monday, Polish police said. He had been wounded in a shootout with officers after opening fire Saturday afternoon and had been in critical condition.

The BBC reported that armed officers reached the scene quickly and shot the suspect within three minutes of the attack beginning, which officials said prevented a further massacre. Six people were confirmed killed: four women and two men. Four were Polish, and the others were a British national and an Austrian woman. The Guardian said 17 people were injured, while the BBC counted 16 people taken to hospital, including the attacker. Five were foreign nationals and two were police officers.

Police said three people found dead at the gunman's home were his father, 53, mother, 52, and sister, 21. Polish media reported he had a firearms permit and may have taken the weapons from the family home, according to the BBC.

Prosecutors opened a terrorism investigation. Officials said he appeared inspired by far-right ideologies. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński described him as holding "very radical" and "ultra-nationalistic" views. An interior ministry spokeswoman, Karolina Galecka, said emblems on his clothing were being analysed by specialists and declined to say more.

Poland began two days of national mourning. Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Poland had not had such drastic cases of terrorism before. The Guardian noted the attack followed school stabbings in October that officials linked to extremist content online. Main Market Square reopened Sunday evening.

Nvidia has opened an independent investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang's relationship with a businesswoman whom US intelligence agencies reportedly believe is a Chinese spy, CNBC reported. In an email to staff on Sunday, Huang said he had an affair with the woman. "I was unfaithful to my wife," he wrote. "There is no excuse for what I did."

According to reports in The New York Times and the Financial Times, cited by CNBC, intelligence agencies are concerned that the woman, Alice Huang, has been passing information to Beijing. She is affiliated with a cloud company and Nvidia customer called Megaspeed. Megaspeed has been accused of helping restricted Chinese companies obtain Nvidia AI chips, and Nvidia representatives said it had already been investigated for evading export controls.

Nvidia's board said it has no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, but that its inquiry would examine "all available information." A company spokesperson said Huang is committed to continuing as CEO without interruption.

The story lands amid a US-China trade dispute in which Nvidia is central. The US restricts exports of its most advanced AI chips to China but has approved some older, slower models. Huang has pushed for broader exports to China and has aligned with President Donald Trump on AI policy.

Several dates are ahead. Three House Republican committee chairs asked Huang last Wednesday to attend a closed-door briefing with lawmakers on Nov. 18. Nvidia reports third-quarter earnings on Nov. 17 and holds a major conference in Washington at the end of the month.

Pope Leo XIV said on Sunday that Argentina's economy must serve everyone, in a speech in Buenos Aires that The Guardian and the BBC both described as a pointed critique of President Javier Milei's austerity measures. Leo had just arrived on the second stop of a 12-day Latin America tour, three weeks after lung cancer surgery.

"The economy must be at the service of the people, rather than people being at the service of the economy," he said. He spoke of those who "despite hard work, nonetheless struggle to meet their household's needs" and called for particular concern for people affected by illness, dependency and disability. Both outlets read that as a veiled reference to cuts to disability assistance. He also said strengthening democracy requires a "willingness to listen" and "careful use of words," and that those in authority must "acknowledge the limits of the power entrusted to them."

The BBC reported that Milei said his government was working to avoid "punishing the Argentines of tomorrow in order to benefit the Argentines of today." In his own address he defended his libertarian policies, saying the rights to life, liberty and property are the backbone of the constitution. He also called the late Pope Francis an "exceptional figure," although he had earlier insulted him.

The Guardian said Milei came to office promising to tame inflation by shrinking the welfare state, and that poverty rose to 32.3% in September. It said he keeps a loyal base for sharply reducing inflation. The local Catholic church has criticized his treatment of social services as a budget item.
Leo will visit a home for disabled people and a prison and celebrate three open-air masses. The church expects 7 million people at the events.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that the war with Iran is unpopular but necessary, telling reporters in Florida that President Donald Trump "identified a very real threat" and worked to stop Iran from pursuing a nuclear weapon, according to Al Jazeera.

On diplomacy, Rubio said, "I wouldn't say we're at the verge of a breakthrough." He said Trump prefers a diplomatic solution but that Iranian demands are "not just unacceptable, but in some cases, outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic."

Trump said he mostly agreed with Vice President JD Vance's recent comments blaming the war for the Republican midterm defeat, but did not regret going to war. He said it "will go down as one of the best things we ever did." In a phone interview with CNN he said that if Washington sees progress and Iran signs a "strong agreement," it is "highly unlikely" the US will need to resume strikes.

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi wrote on X that it was "time for the White House to make its own" decision and that "American voters have made their choice." He said Tehran's "2-day proposal stands: meet the requirements, including end to war on all fronts, and you will see results." Iran has offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping within two days if the US meets its conditions. He also warned of a forceful response if the US chooses war.

Next, Trump is scheduled to meet Qatar's prime minister and foreign minister at the White House on Monday. The Associated Press reported that Tehran is reviewing Qatari proposals aimed at narrowing differences with Washington.

A drone attack on the Khor Mor gasfield in Iraq's Kurdish region caused a fire and cut power across much of the area on Sunday night, according to Iraqi and Kurdish officials cited by Al Jazeera. The attack left more than 70 percent of the region without electricity.

Omid Ahmed, spokesperson for the Kurdistan Regional Government's Ministry of Electricity, said the strike suspended gas supply to power plants in Erbil, Sulaimaniyah, Bazian, Chamchamal and Duhok, the Iraqi News Agency reported. He said it knocked between 2,500 and 2,800 megawatts of generation off the grid. The ministry said it would supply critical facilities such as hospitals and water treatment plants by running hydroelectric stations and plants that use alternative fuel.

Al Jazeera's Peter Smith, reporting from Baghdad, cited security sources as saying an explosive-laden drone hit the Khor Mor gas storage facility, cutting grid capacity by 70 to 80 percent. Al Jazeera's fact-checking agency Sanad verified footage of smoke and flames near the gasfield in Sulaimaniyah governorate.

Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said an initial assessment found no casualties, according to the Iraqi News Agency. He directed that a joint investigative committee be formed with authorities in the Kurdish region to examine the circumstances of the attack.

It was not clear who was responsible or whether the attack was related to the US and Israeli war on Iran. Al Jazeera noted that a drone strike hit the same facility last year, and no group claimed responsibility. The investigation is the next development to watch.

The International Maritime Organization has recorded the deaths of at least 25 seafarers since the US-Israeli war on Iran began on February 28, Al Jazeera reported. Many of those killed were Indian citizens. The IMO has also counted at least 129 incidents involving ships, which have been hit by missiles, projectiles and naval mines.

On Sunday, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said three "rogue oil tankers travelling an unauthorised route" in the Strait of Hormuz suffered "explosions and severe fires." Before the war, roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption passed through the strait. Iran essentially closed it and warned that ships sailing without authorization could be targeted, while the US has blockaded Iranian ports. At least 31 vessels were hit in October.

The victims are largely civilian merchant sailors. At least 16 Indians have been killed, including three in US strikes on commercial vessels near Oman in June, which led New Delhi to summon a senior American diplomat. Two Filipino crew members died in September when the tanker Sidr was hit. In May, the head of Iran's merchant marine union said at least 44 Iranian seafarers had been killed.

The International Chamber of Shipping called it "unacceptable" that seafarers have been "placed in harm's way" and urged all parties to protect them. It said the war has also harmed mental health. About 6,000 seafarers remained stranded near the strait in October, the IMO said.

In March, unions and shipping companies agreed that seafarers could refuse to enter designated danger zones and receive repatriation and two months' basic pay. Al Jazeera noted those protections do not necessarily cover every seafarer.

Asian stock markets rebounded on Monday after a tech rout last week, Al Jazeera reported. The rout was triggered by the Democratic Party's sweeping victory in the US midterm elections. The gains followed a rebound on Wall Street on Friday.

As of 04:00 GMT, Tokyo's Nikkei 225 was up 3.45 percent, Taipei's Taiex was up 5.72 percent and Seoul's Kospi was up 1.68 percent. Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index was up 0.19 percent. Futures for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq 100 were up 0.60 percent and 0.59 percent.

Those futures had dipped earlier after Nvidia said it would investigate its CEO, Jensen Huang, over a romantic relationship with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia's board said it had confidence in Huang and no reason to believe national security or company secrets were compromised, but that an independent inquiry would examine "all available information." The board said Huang supported the inquiry and pledged full cooperation.

The earlier losses were large. The midterm results prompted a $2.5 trillion sell-off on Wall Street on Thursday amid concerns that Democratic-controlled legislatures could slow the rollout of data centers used to power AI. The rout spread to Asia on Friday, with the Nikkei 225 and Kospi plunging about 6 percent and 9 percent, and the Hang Seng Index dropping more than 1 percent.

Al Jazeera's report did not say whether the Monday gains would hold. The Nvidia inquiry remains open, and investors will be watching it alongside how the new Democratic majorities approach data center policy.

China's producer prices rose 5.7% in October from a year earlier, the fastest pace since June 2022, CNBC reported. It was the third straight month of acceleration. Economists polled by Reuters had expected 5.3%. The increase was driven by a sharp rise in prices in the mining and raw materials industries.
Zhang Zhiwei, president and chief economist at Pinpoint Asset Management, told CNBC the rise was driven by very strong external demand.

Consumer prices told a different story. Consumer inflation slowed to 0.7% in October, its first slowdown after two straight monthly increases. That missed the 0.8% economists expected and was below September's 0.9%. Core inflation, which strips out food and energy prices, fell to 0.8% from 1%.

Dong Lijuan, chief statistician of the urban division at China's National Bureau of Statistics, said gasoline was the largest contributor to the rise in consumer prices. A sharper than expected fall in food prices offset it.

The Chinese economy has shown some signs of expansion, CNBC noted. It grew faster than expected in the third quarter, and retail sales sharply beat forecasts in September. The CSI 300 index gained 0.56% after the data release.

Zhang said domestic demand remains weak, largely because of the property market, where he saw "no clear sign of stabilization" yet. He said that was weighing on household confidence and local government revenue, and that overall economic momentum "hasn't really seen [a] clear sign of recovery."

Mexican authorities have arrested Rafael Alvarez, known as "R2," an alleged leader in the Jalisco New Generation Cartel (CJNG), one of the country's two main criminal groups. According to Mexico's Navy, he was detained on Sunday in an operation in Zapopan, in the Guadalajara metropolitan area, based on intelligence shared by the US Drug Enforcement Administration.

Alvarez is suspected of heading the CJNG cell known as "Los Rs." Security Minister Omar Garcia Harfuch said the cell is mainly linked to extortion, drug trafficking, homicide, illegal deprivation of liberty, kidnapping and attacks against authorities, and that its extortion victims included business owners and avocado producers. Harfuch said on X that Alvarez was wounded in a shootout during the arrest and is receiving medical care.

Harfuch said Alvarez faces an outstanding arrest warrant in Mexico for aggravated homicide and a separate warrant for extradition to the US. Mexico's National Intelligence Center and other authorities also took part, and 19 other people were captured. Al Jazeera reports that Alvarez is linked to the killing of at least 19 people, including last year's murder of Carlos Manzo, the mayor of Uruapan in Michoacan state.

The US government designated the CJNG a foreign terrorist organisation in 2025. The group competes with the Sinaloa Cartel for drug trafficking into the US. Since the death of founder Nemesio "El Mencho" Oseguera in a military operation in February, several of its top leaders have been apprehended, Al Jazeera reports. Even so, there are still reports of kidnapping for ransom where the cartels operate, and an estimated 134,000 people are believed missing across Mexico, with Jalisco recording the highest numbers.

Bangladesh's ousted prime minister, Sheikh Hasina, has requested a new passport and identity card to allow her to return from self-imposed exile in India, according to Al Jazeera. She has lived in India for two years, and the request is described as the clearest sign that she plans to keep her promise to return in December.

Hasina told Reuters she intends to surrender before a court in Bangladesh. Her aides said on Monday that the date would be announced once various formalities were completed. Her letter to the Bangladeshi government, cited by Reuters, asked that her request be processed "expeditiously" on the basis of her Bangladeshi nationality.

Bangladesh's war crimes court sentenced Hasina to death in absentia last November for ordering a deadly crackdown on the student protests that swept the country in 2024. As many as 1,400 people may have been killed in those protests, according to United Nations estimates. Al Jazeera's report does not include her response to the verdict. She was ousted by a student-led mass movement that began after the Supreme Court restored a job quota system that had prioritised the descendants of the country's liberation activists.

Hasina is the daughter of Bangladesh's founder and first president, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. She served as prime minister from 1996 to 2001 and again from 2009 to 2024, making her the country's longest-ruling leader. Al Jazeera says her return raises the prospect of renewed legal and political issues in a country of 127 million people. She still has support among some Bangladeshis, and her return could affect government efforts to stabilise the country and economy after two years of disruption. It could also smooth relations with India, which deteriorated sharply when she fled there.

Scientists say the world is on course for its hottest year on record as COP31, the latest UN climate summit, opens Monday in Antalya, Turkey. Berkeley Earth, an independent US research group, told BBC News it is 95% confident that 2026 will surpass the previous record set in 2024. The EU's Copernicus climate service confirmed on Friday that October was the hottest on record.

The UN's World Meteorological Organization was more cautious, forecasting that 2026 will be among the four warmest years on record. It said 2027 will bring no let-up because an unusually powerful El Niño will continue into next year. Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said El Niño does not add new heat but releases heat from the ocean, which is the warmest ever measured.

The BBC reports the world is currently on track for 2.8C of warming above pre-industrial levels by the end of the century, all but guaranteeing the Paris Agreement's 1.5C goal will be exceeded. UN climate chief Simon Stiell is expected to tell governments that no single COP is a silver bullet, but that the urgency of the moment must drive them forward.

Negotiators will meet for two weeks. The Turkish government wants discussions to focus on a new electrification goal and on cutting waste. The BBC says the talks are likely to split countries. Early drafts of the EU position say it would back an electrification goal only if countries could not meet it using gas, while Saudi Arabia and Russia have previously pushed the interim use of gas as a cleaner alternative to coal. The BBC understands the UK government is reluctant to set new goals and thinks the focus should be on existing agreements.

NASA says the Antarctic ozone hole has reached its 2026 maximum, ranking seventh largest by area in 48 years of monitoring. It was not as deep as other large holes on record. The ranking is based on the hole's mean size from September 7 to October 13, the peak depletion season, and NASA says the day of its annual maximum area was September 18.

NASA attributes the large area to an unusually strong Antarctic polar vortex, which created ideal conditions for ozone depletion. Year-to-year changes in area and depth are caused by variations in stratospheric temperature and circulation, and colder conditions produce a larger hole with lower ozone values at its core.

The word hole is a metaphor, NASA explains: no place is empty of ozone, and scientists use the term for the area where concentrations fall below 220 Dobson Units. The deepest hole occurred in 1994, when concentrations fell to 73 Dobson Units on September 30, and the largest by area occurred in 2006. Records in depth and area have never occurred in the same year.

The hole led to the 1987 Montreal Protocol, which phased out ozone-depleting chemicals such as chlorofluorocarbons. NASA says about 80 percent of the chlorine in the stratosphere today comes from human sources. Models suggest chlorine and other ozone-depleting substances will not return to pre-1980 levels until later this century, and scientists estimate the Antarctic ozone layer will return to 1980 levels in the 2070s. NASA notes that in 2019 abnormal weather limited depletion and produced the smallest hole since 1982.

Former President Joe Biden said on Sunday that he will need to limit promotional events for his memoir because his cancer treatment sometimes slows him down, Fox News reports. The book, titled "Promise Me, America," is due out on Nov. 17.

According to Fox News, the memoir reflects on Biden's four years in the White House. It covers the COVID-19 pandemic, the aftermath of the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol riot, domestic legislation, global diplomacy and his decision to run for re-election before stepping aside in 2024, including the personal deliberations behind ending that bid.

Biden was diagnosed in May 2025 with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had spread to his bones. In a post on X he said: "Some days are better than others. It hasn't stopped me. But sometimes it slows me down." He said that means he will not be able to do as many conversations about the book as he had hoped, but that he is hopeful "the words on the page speak for themselves."

He said his doctors continue to be encouraged by how he has responded to treatment, and he thanked people for their prayers and well wishes. He described the book as covering "the challenges we faced, the decisions I made, and why I made them," and said it is about his faith in the American people. He also recalled his father telling him, "When you get knocked down, get up." The page text does not say which promotional events have been scheduled.

Moldova has officially launched a new power line connecting it to neighbouring Romania and the European grid, a project meant to reduce its reliance on Russian energy, Al Jazeera reports. President Maia Sandu spoke at the inauguration ceremony on Sunday in the capital, Chisinau, and said the project strengthens transmission capacity and diversifies supply.

The 400-kilowatt extra-high-voltage line runs from the city of Vulcanesti to Chisinau and allows Moldova to cut reliance on the Cuciurgan thermal power plant in Transnistria. Dubbed the "energy independence line," it opened two years after the date Moldovan authorities initially promised. Sandu said two more lines to Romania are on the way. European Commissioner for Energy Marta Kos, who attended, said Moldova could now "buy energy where it is cheapest."

Sandu said on X that "for decades, Moscow used energy to blackmail us" and that Moldova now buys zero Russian gas. She also said that whenever Moldova chooses something other than what Moscow wants, Moscow threatens to cut its electricity. A Russian response was not included in the page text.

Moldova, a country of 2.6 million people, received most of its gas from Russia via the pro-Moscow separatist region of Transnistria and pipelines through Ukraine. Last month, parliament approved a state of emergency until November 20 as the government tries to ease gas shortages amid soaring world energy prices. Some in Europe have blamed Moscow for the price rises, accusing it of withholding supplies.

Al Jazeera adds that European-aligned Black Sea states report renewed attacks allegedly carried out by Russia. Romania blamed Russia for a drone strike that sank a cargo ship, and NATO said it would send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the region.

Heavy smog blanketed New Delhi on Monday after firecrackers lit up the Indian capital during Diwali celebrations, worsening the city's seasonal pollution crisis, Al Jazeera reports. Diwali, the Hindu festival of lights, was celebrated across India on Sunday. Despite restrictions on fireworks, residents set off firecrackers throughout the evening, releasing smoke and fine particulate matter into the air.

On Monday morning the Air Quality Index exceeded 350 in several parts of the capital. That is categorised as "severe" and poses significant health risks, according to Al Jazeera, which cites the World Health Organization's recommended exposure thresholds.

Last month, India's Supreme Court put restrictions in place to limit Diwali pollution. They allowed only approved "green firecrackers," under specified conditions, during three-hour windows on Saturday and Sunday. Al Jazeera notes that the approved crackers produce fewer emissions but are not pollution-free. The page text does not say whether authorities have taken action over violations of the rules.

Air quality was already poor before the festival. On Wednesday, days before Diwali, air monitors showed pollution in New Delhi surging to more than 30 times the WHO's recommended daily limit. New Delhi, home to 30 million people, persistently ranks among the world's most polluted capital cities.

The problem is made worse in winter, when cooler temperatures, low wind speeds and stagnant atmospheric conditions prevent pollutants from dispersing. According to India's Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, vehicles account for 23 percent of the city's winter pollution and biomass burning, including farm stubble fires, for 20 percent. The resulting haze can linger over the capital and surrounding areas for days.

A new DemosAU/PremierNational poll, first published by the Herald Sun on Monday, puts Victorian Labor's primary vote at an all-time low of 18%, down seven points. That places it third behind the Coalition on 33% and One Nation on 21%. The Greens rose three points since September to 17%. The Coalition leads Labor 56-44 on a two-party preferred basis, compared with 52-48 in September.

DemosAU's head of research, George Hasanakos, said he "double, triple, quadruple checked" the result. The poll had 1,562 respondents, an effective sample of 818 and a margin of error of 3.4%. He said that if it were replicated on election night, many contests would be between the Liberals or Nationals and One Nation, producing a clear Coalition majority, and that One Nation would need to poll very well because Labor and Greens preferences would flow to the Liberals.

Ben Carroll repeatedly refused to say whether he was worried about the poll. He said he was focused on fighting for working people ahead of the November 28 election and that the alternative was a Liberal-One Nation government that would shrink the economy. According to the Guardian, Labor campaign headquarters is treating the result as an "outlier" and points to other public polls that have the party's primary vote in the 20s.

Several Labor MPs, who were not authorised to speak publicly, told Guardian Australia they have serious concerns. One said the caucus was "really angry and deflated," and another called the recent focus on crime a "diabolically stupid strategy." Carroll announced $204m for a youth rehabilitation detention program and $70m for 200 more police reservists.

Opposition leader Jess Wilson said her party is focused on getting tough on crime, including through Aidan's Law, and Carroll matched that commitment. Separately, Pauline Hanson rejected reports that former campaign director Sean Black still secretly works for One Nation in Victoria.

A BBC team spent months trying to gain access to the drug gangs of Marseille, France's second city, and found ruthless groups that lure vulnerable young people with promises of easy money and then trap them in drug dealing, brutality and exploitation. The team reports that gangs now use social media to recruit hitmen.

One case heard in a French court this year illustrates the pattern. In 2022 a woman who bought hashish on the Frais-Vallon estate was handed a note by the young seller reading, "We're being held captive and need help. We are 15-years-old." The court heard that the two boys had sought paid work from the gang and were later accused of shortfalls in takings, beaten, filmed naked as blackmail and, in one case, raped. Six men have since received heavy sentences.

The BBC says the city's most powerful gang, DZ Mafia, emerged victorious from a bloody turf war. In 2023 it became the first French gang to release video statements, marketing itself like a brand, according to anti-drug trafficking unit head Dimitri Zoulas. He says cocaine users in France are expected soon to reach two million, up from 600,000 in 2017, and that drug smuggling generates €7bn a year and involves 200,000 people.

Authorities say the number of minors caught up in trafficking is rising, with more than 10,000 children involved in some way during 2025. The BBC found DZ Mafia now recruits young people from across France to carry out kidnap, torture and murder, typically controlled by kingpins in prison or overseas.

Karine Brouillard described how her son Hugo, who had told his family he had a restaurant job near Marseille, was brought to a doctor with a bullet to the head in 2023. Police believe he was involved with a gang in Quartier Nord. The BBC team entered the area with a local resident and was stopped at a gang checkpoint within seconds, released only after agreeing to stop filming.
